imc-1997-01.title: Squeeze between Riemann sums of $\ln$
imc-1997-01.body:
Write $L_n=\frac1n\sum_{k=1}^n\ln\left(\frac kn+\varepsilon_n\right)$.

**A Riemann-sum estimate.** Let $\delta\ge0$ and $h(x)=\ln(x+\delta)$, an increasing function on $(-\delta,\infty)$. For $1\le k\le n$, monotonicity gives
$$\int_{(k-1)/n}^{k/n}h(x)\,dx\ \le\ \frac1n\,h\!\left(\frac kn\right)\ \le\ \int_{k/n}^{(k+1)/n}h(x)\,dx$$
(the left integral is an improper but convergent integral when $\delta=0$, $k=1$). Summing over $k$,
$$\int_0^1\ln(x+\delta)\,dx\ \le\ \frac1n\sum_{k=1}^n\ln\left(\frac kn+\delta\right)\ \le\ \int_{1/n}^{1+1/n}\ln(x+\delta)\,dx. \tag{$*$}$$

**Lower bound.** Since $\varepsilon_n>0$ and $\ln$ is increasing, $L_n\ge\frac1n\sum_{k=1}^n\ln\frac kn\ge\int_0^1\ln x\,dx=-1$ by $(*)$ with $\delta=0$.

**Upper bound.** Fix $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$. For $n$ large, $\varepsilon_n\le\varepsilon$, so by $(*)$ with $\delta=\varepsilon$,
$$L_n\le\frac1n\sum_{k=1}^n\ln\left(\frac kn+\varepsilon\right)\le\int_{1/n+\varepsilon}^{1+1/n+\varepsilon}\ln t\,dt\ \xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}\ \int_{\varepsilon}^{1+\varepsilon}\ln t\,dt .$$
With $\int\ln t\,dt=t\ln t-t$,
$$\int_\varepsilon^{1+\varepsilon}\ln t\,dt=(1+\varepsilon)\ln(1+\varepsilon)-\varepsilon\ln\varepsilon-1=:\,u(\varepsilon),$$
so $\limsup_n L_n\le u(\varepsilon)$ for every $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$. Since $\varepsilon\ln\varepsilon\to0$ and $(1+\varepsilon)\ln(1+\varepsilon)\to0$ as $\varepsilon\to0^+$, $u(\varepsilon)\to-1$, hence $\limsup L_n\le-1$.

Together with $L_n\ge-1$ we get $\lim L_n=-1$.

**Answer: $-1$**

imc-1997-01.title: Lower bound via Stirling
imc-1997-01.body:
The lower bound can also be seen without integrals: $L_n\ge\frac1n\sum_{k=1}^n\ln\frac kn=\frac{\ln n!}{n}-\ln n$, and by Stirling's formula $\ln n!=n\ln n-n+O(\ln n)$, so this tends to $-1$.

For the upper bound, fix $\varepsilon>0$; for large $n$, $L_n\le\frac1n\sum_{k=1}^n\ln\left(\frac kn+\varepsilon\right)$, and the right-hand side is a Riemann sum of the continuous function $\ln(x+\varepsilon)$ on $[0,1]$, so it tends to $\int_0^1\ln(x+\varepsilon)\,dx$, which tends to $\int_0^1\ln x\,dx=-1$ as $\varepsilon\to0^+$ (monotone convergence). Hence $\limsup L_n\le-1\le\liminf L_n$.

**Answer: $-1$**

imc-1997-02.title: Express the partial sums through those of the original series
imc-1997-02.body:
Let $S_N=a_1+\dots+a_N$ and $S=\lim S_N$.

**a) Yes.** After $a_1$, the rearranged series runs through the blocks $B_m=(a_{2^m},a_{2^m-1},\dots,a_{2^{m-1}+1})$, $m=1,2,\dots$ (each block contains the indices $2^{m-1}+1,\dots,2^m$ in decreasing order). Hence a partial sum that ends after the first $k$ terms of block $B_m$ ($1\le k\le 2^{m-1}$) equals
$$S_{2^{m-1}}+\bigl(a_{2^m}+a_{2^m-1}+\dots+a_{2^m-k+1}\bigr)=S_{2^{m-1}}+S_{2^m}-S_{2^m-k}.$$
All three indices $2^{m-1},\,2^m,\,2^m-k$ are $\ge 2^{m-1}$. Given $\varepsilon>0$ choose $N_0$ with $|S_N-S|<\varepsilon$ for $N\ge N_0$; if $2^{m-1}\ge N_0$, the partial sum above differs from $S+S-S=S$ by less than $3\varepsilon$. So all partial sums of the rearranged series far enough out are within $3\varepsilon$ of $S$: the series converges (to $S$).

**b) No.** Here, after $a_1,a_2$, the series runs through the blocks of indices $2^m+1,\dots,2^{m+1}$ ($m\ge1$), each block listing first its odd indices and then its even indices (e.g. $5,7,6,8$ and $9,11,13,15,10,12,14,16$).

Take $a_n=\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{\sqrt n}$; $\sum a_n$ converges by the Leibniz test, and the odd-indexed terms are positive. The partial sum of the rearranged series that ends after the odd terms of block $m$ equals
$$S_{2^m}+\sum_{\substack{2^m<j<2^{m+1}\\ j\text{ odd}}}\frac1{\sqrt j}\ \ge\ S_{2^m}+2^{m-1}\cdot\frac1{\sqrt{2^{m+1}}}=S_{2^m}+2^{(m-3)/2},$$
because the block contains $2^{m-1}$ odd indices, each $<2^{m+1}$. Since $S_{2^m}\to S$ and $2^{(m-3)/2}\to\infty$, these partial sums tend to $+\infty$, so the rearranged series diverges. ∎

imc-1997-03.title: Factor with a cube root of unity
imc-1997-03.body:
Let $\omega=-\frac12+\frac{\sqrt3}2i$, so $\omega^3=1$, $|\omega|=1$, $\overline\omega=\omega^2$ and $1+\omega+\overline\omega=0$, i.e. $1+\overline\omega=-\omega$.

Put $S=A+\omega B$; since $A,B$ are real, $\overline S=A+\overline\omega B$. Then
$$S\overline S=(A+\omega B)(A+\overline\omega B)=A^2+\overline\omega AB+\omega BA+\omega\overline\omega B^2=(A^2+B^2)+\overline\omega AB+\omega BA.$$
Using $A^2+B^2=AB$,
$$S\overline S=(1+\overline\omega)AB+\omega BA=-\omega AB+\omega BA=\omega\,(BA-AB).$$
Take determinants. On the left, $\det(S\overline S)=\det S\cdot\det\overline S=\det S\cdot\overline{\det S}=|\det S|^2$, a real number. On the right, $\det\bigl(\omega(BA-AB)\bigr)=\omega^n\det(BA-AB)$, where $d=\det(BA-AB)$ is real and, by assumption, nonzero. Therefore $\omega^n=|\det S|^2/d$ is real.

But $\omega^n\in\{1,\omega,\omega^2\}$ and $\omega,\omega^2$ are not real; hence $\omega^n=1$, which happens exactly when $3\mid n$. ∎

imc-1997-04.title: Greedy construction and tail bounds
imc-1997-04.body:
Call a sequence of positive integers with $n_{i+1}\ge n_i^2$ *admissible*.

**Lemma (tail bounds).** For an integer $M\ge2$, $\prod_{j\ge0}\bigl(1+M^{-2^j}\bigr)=\sum_{s\ge0}M^{-s}=\frac M{M-1}$, because expanding the product gives every power $M^{-s}$ exactly once (binary expansion of $s$). If $(n_k,n_{k+1},\dots)$ is admissible with $n_k=M\ge2$, then $n_{k+i}\ge M^{2^i}$ by induction, so the tail $T_k=\prod_{j\ge k}(1+\frac1{n_j})$ satisfies
$$1+\frac1{n_k}<T_k\le\frac{n_k}{n_k-1}=1+\frac1{n_k-1},$$
with equality on the right **iff** $n_{j+1}=n_j^2$ for all $j\ge k$. (The left inequality is strict since the later factors are $>1$. Also, an admissible product whose value is $<2$ cannot have $n_1=1$, since then the first factor alone is $2$; and $n_1\ge2$ gives $n_k\ge2$ for all $k$.)

**a) Uniqueness.** The intervals $J_n=\bigl(1+\frac1n,\,1+\frac1{n-1}\bigr]$, $n\ge2$, are pairwise disjoint. By the lemma, $T_k\in J_{n_k}$, so $n_k$ is determined by $T_k$. Now $T_1=\alpha$ determines $n_1$, then $T_2=\alpha/(1+\frac1{n_1})$ determines $n_2$, and so on: the representation is unique.

**a) Existence (greedy).** Put $\theta_0=\alpha\in(1,2)$. Given $\theta_{k-1}\in(1,2)$, let $n_k\ge2$ be the integer with $\theta_{k-1}\in J_{n_k}$ (the $J_n$ cover $(1,2]$), and set $\theta_k=\theta_{k-1}/(1+\frac1{n_k})$. Then $\theta_k>1$ and
$$\theta_k\le\frac{1+\frac1{n_k-1}}{1+\frac1{n_k}}=\frac{n_k}{n_k-1}\cdot\frac{n_k}{n_k+1}=1+\frac1{n_k^2-1}\ (<2).$$
Hence $1+\frac1{n_{k+1}}<\theta_k\le1+\frac1{n_k^2-1}$ gives $n_{k+1}>n_k^2-1$, i.e. $n_{k+1}\ge n_k^2$: the sequence is admissible. As $n_k\ge2^{2^{k-1}}\to\infty$, $\theta_k\to1$, and since $\alpha=\theta_k\prod_{i=1}^k(1+\frac1{n_i})$, the infinite product converges to $\alpha$.

**b)** If $n_{k+1}=n_k^2$ for all $k\ge m$, the lemma gives $T_m=\frac{n_m}{n_m-1}$, so $\alpha=\prod_{i<m}(1+\frac1{n_i})\cdot T_m$ is rational.

Conversely let $\alpha=p/q$ with positive integers $p>q$, and suppose that the squaring property fails from every index on. By the equality case of the lemma, $T_k<\frac{n_k}{n_k-1}$ for **every** $k$. Define $p_1=p$, $q_1=q$ and $p_{k+1}=p_kn_k$, $q_{k+1}=q_k(n_k+1)$; since $T_{k+1}=T_k\cdot\frac{n_k}{n_k+1}$, induction gives $T_k=p_k/q_k$. As $T_k>1$, $d_k=p_k-q_k$ is a positive integer. But
$$d_{k+1}-d_k=p_kn_k-q_kn_k-q_k-p_k+q_k=(n_k-1)p_k-n_kq_k<0,$$
because $\frac{p_k}{q_k}=T_k<\frac{n_k}{n_k-1}$. So $(d_k)$ is a strictly decreasing sequence of positive integers — a contradiction. Hence $n_{k+1}=n_k^2$ for all $k$ from some $m$ on. ∎

imc-1997-05.title: Convexity and pairing of unit steps
imc-1997-05.body:
**a)** Let $1\le p<\infty$ and $\varphi(t)=|t|^p$, a convex function; put $F(z)=\sum_i\varphi(z_i)=\|z\|_p^p$. We use two elementary facts about a convex $\varphi$.

*Fact 1.* For real $s$ and an integer $y\ge1$: $\varphi(s+y)-\varphi(s)\ge y\,[\varphi(s+1)-\varphi(s)]$; for an integer $y\le-1$: $\varphi(s+y)-\varphi(s)\ge|y|\,[\varphi(s-1)-\varphi(s)]$. Indeed, $\varphi(s+y)-\varphi(s)=\sum_{t=0}^{y-1}[\varphi(s+t+1)-\varphi(s+t)]$ and, by convexity, the slopes of consecutive unit chords are nondecreasing, so each term is at least the first one. The case $y\le-1$ is symmetric.

*Fact 2.* If $u\le s\le t\le v$ and $s+t=u+v$, then $\varphi(s)+\varphi(t)\le\varphi(u)+\varphi(v)$. (If $u<v$, write $s=\lambda u+(1-\lambda)v$, $t=(1-\lambda)u+\lambda v$ with $\lambda\in[0,1]$, apply convexity to each and add.)

Now let $x$ be as in a) (in fact we only need $\max x_i-\min x_i\le1$) and $y\in\mathbb Z^n_0$, $y\ne0$. Let $P=\{i:y_i>0\}$, $N=\{j:y_j<0\}$; since $\sum y_i=0$, both are nonempty and $\sum_{i\in P}y_i=\sum_{j\in N}|y_j|=:K$. Set $D^+_i=\varphi(x_i+1)-\varphi(x_i)$ and $D^-_j=\varphi(x_j-1)-\varphi(x_j)$. By Fact 1,
$$F(x+y)-F(x)\ \ge\ \sum_{i\in P}y_iD^+_i+\sum_{j\in N}|y_j|D^-_j\ \ge\ K\Bigl(\min_{i}D^+_i+\min_{j}D^-_j\Bigr).$$
It remains to show $D^+_i+D^-_j\ge0$ for all indices $i,j$, i.e. $\varphi(x_i+1)+\varphi(x_j-1)\ge\varphi(x_i)+\varphi(x_j)$. Put $a=x_i$, $b=x_j$. Since $|a-b|\le\max x-\min x\le1$, we have $b-1\le a$ and $b-1\le b$, while $a+1\ge b$ and $a+1\ge a$. So $b-1\le\min(a,b)\le\max(a,b)\le a+1$ and $(b-1)+(a+1)=a+b$; Fact 2 gives the claim.

Hence $F(x+y)\ge F(x)$, i.e. $\|x+y\|_p\ge\|x\|_p$ for all $p\in[1,\infty)$. For $p=\infty$ let $p\to\infty$: in $\mathbb R^n$, $\|z\|_p\to\|z\|_\infty$, and the inequality passes to the limit.

**b)** Fix $p\in(0,1)$ and an integer $m\ge1$; let $n=3m$,
$$x=(\underbrace{\tfrac23,\dots,\tfrac23}_{m},\underbrace{-\tfrac13,\dots,-\tfrac13}_{2m}),\qquad y=(\underbrace{-1,\dots,-1}_{m},m,\underbrace{0,\dots,0}_{2m-1}).$$
Then $\sum x_i=\frac{2m}3-\frac{2m}3=0$, $\max x_i-\min x_i=1$, $y\in\mathbb Z^n_0$, and
$$x+y=(\underbrace{-\tfrac13,\dots,-\tfrac13}_{m},m-\tfrac13,\underbrace{-\tfrac13,\dots,-\tfrac13}_{2m-1}).$$
Thus
$$\|x\|_p^p-\|x+y\|_p^p=m\Bigl(\bigl(\tfrac23\bigr)^p-\bigl(\tfrac13\bigr)^p\Bigr)+\bigl(\tfrac13\bigr)^p-\bigl(m-\tfrac13\bigr)^p>mc-m^p,$$
where $c=(\frac23)^p-(\frac13)^p>0$. Because $p<1$, $mc-m^p=m^p(cm^{1-p}-1)>0$ as soon as $m^{1-p}>1/c$. For such $m$, $\|x\|_p>\|x+y\|_p$. ∎

imc-1997-06.title: Counterexample, then induction on the sizes
imc-1997-06.body:
**a) No.** For $n\ge1$ let $A_n=\{1,3,5,\dots,2n-1,2n\}$ and $B_n=\{2,4,\dots,2n,2n+1\}$, and $\mathcal F=\{A_n,B_n:n\ge1\}$.
- Any two $A$'s contain $1$; any two $B$'s contain $2$.
- $A_n\cap B_m$: if $n\le m$, the even number $2n\le 2m$ lies in both; if $n>m$, the odd number $2m+1\le2n-1$ lies in both.

So $\mathcal F$ is pairwise intersecting. But $A_n\cap B_n=\{2n\}$ (the only even element of $A_n$ is $2n$, the only odd element of $B_n$ is $2n+1>2n-1$). For a finite $Y$ pick $n$ with $2n>\max Y$; then $A_n\cap B_n\cap Y=\varnothing$.

**b) Yes.** We prove a stronger statement.

*Claim.* Let $\mathcal F,\mathcal G$ be families of finite subsets of $\mathbb N$ such that every $A\in\mathcal F$ has exactly $r$ elements, every $B\in\mathcal G$ has exactly $s$ elements, and $A\cap B\ne\varnothing$ for all $A\in\mathcal F$, $B\in\mathcal G$. Then there is a finite $Y$ with $A\cap B\cap Y\ne\varnothing$ for all $A\in\mathcal F,B\in\mathcal G$.

Taking $\mathcal G=\mathcal F$ gives b) (including the case $A=B$).

*Proof* by strong induction on $r+s$. If $\mathcal F$ or $\mathcal G$ is empty, take $Y=\varnothing$. Otherwise fix $A_0\in\mathcal F$, $B_0\in\mathcal G$ and let $U=A_0\cup B_0$ (finite). Every $A\in\mathcal F$ meets $B_0$, so $C=A\cap U$ is a nonempty subset of $U$; similarly every $B\in\mathcal G$ has nonempty trace $D=B\cap U$. Let $\mathcal F(C)=\{A\in\mathcal F:A\cap U=C\}$ and $\mathcal G(D)=\{B\in\mathcal G:B\cap U=D\}$. There are finitely many pairs $(C,D)$; it suffices to find a finite $Y_{C,D}$ that works for $\mathcal F(C)$ and $\mathcal G(D)$ (both nonempty), and then take $Y=\bigcup_{C,D}Y_{C,D}$.
- If $C\cap D\ne\varnothing$: every $A\in\mathcal F(C)$, $B\in\mathcal G(D)$ satisfy $A\cap B\cap U=C\cap D\ne\varnothing$, so $Y_{C,D}=U$ works.
- If $C\cap D=\varnothing$: then for $A\in\mathcal F(C)$, $B\in\mathcal G(D)$ the (nonempty) set $A\cap B$ lies outside $U$, so $A\cap B=(A\setminus C)\cap(B\setminus D)$. The families $\{A\setminus C\}$ and $\{B\setminus D\}$ are cross-intersecting and uniform of sizes $r-|C|<r$ and $s-|D|<s$. By the induction hypothesis there is a finite $Y_{C,D}$ with $(A\setminus C)\cap(B\setminus D)\cap Y_{C,D}\ne\varnothing$, hence $A\cap B\cap Y_{C,D}\ne\varnothing$.

(When $r+s$ is minimal the second case cannot occur, since then $A\setminus C$ would be empty yet must meet $B\setminus D$; so no separate base case is needed.) This proves the claim. ∎

imc-1997-07.title: Taylor expansion, then a $C^2$ counterexample
imc-1997-07.body:
Let $c=\frac12f''(0)>0$. Because $f\in C^3$, Taylor's theorem with bounded $f'''$ near $0$ gives, for $|x|\le\delta$,
$$f(x)=cx^2+O(|x|^3),\qquad f'(x)=2cx+O(x^2),\qquad f''(x)=2c+O(|x|).$$
In particular, for small $x\ne0$, $f(x)>0$ and $f'(x)\ne0$, so $g$ is defined there, and by the quotient rule
$$g=\frac{f'\cdot\frac{f'}{2\sqrt f}-\sqrt f\,f''}{f'^2}=\frac{f'^2-2ff''}{2f'^2\sqrt f}.$$
**Numerator:** $f'^2=4c^2x^2+O(|x|^3)$ and $2ff''=2(cx^2+O(|x|^3))(2c+O(|x|))=4c^2x^2+O(|x|^3)$, so $f'^2-2ff''=O(|x|^3)$.

**Denominator:** $f'(x)^2=x^2(2c+O(|x|))^2\ge c^2x^2$ and $f(x)=x^2(c+O(|x|))\ge\frac c2x^2$ for small $|x|$, so $2f'^2\sqrt f\ge2c^2\sqrt{c/2}\,|x|^3$.

Hence $|g(x)|\le K|x|^3/(\kappa|x|^3)=K/\kappa$ near $0$: $g$ is bounded in a neighbourhood of $0$.

**For $C^2$ the statement fails.** Let $f(x)=(x+|x|^{3/2})^2=x^2+2x|x|^{3/2}+|x|^3$. The terms $x^2$, $|x|^3$ and $2x|x|^{3/2}=2\operatorname{sgn}(x)|x|^{5/2}$ are $C^2$ (the last has second derivative $\frac{15}2\operatorname{sgn}(x)|x|^{1/2}$, continuous and $0$ at $0$). So $f\in C^2$, $f\ge0$, $f(0)=f'(0)=0$, $f''(0)=2>0$. For $x>0$: $\sqrt{f(x)}=x+x^{3/2}$ and $f'(x)=2(x+x^{3/2})(1+\frac32\sqrt x)$, so
$$\frac{\sqrt f}{f'}=\frac1{2\left(1+\frac32\sqrt x\right)},\qquad g(x)=-\frac12\cdot\frac{\frac34x^{-1/2}}{\left(1+\frac32\sqrt x\right)^2}\xrightarrow[x\to0^+]{}-\infty .$$
So $g$ is unbounded near $0$. **Answer: bounded for $C^3$; not necessarily for $C^2$.** ∎

imc-1997-08.title: Multiply by a block-triangular matrix
imc-1997-08.body:
Let $I$ be the $n\times n$ identity. From $MM^{-1}=I_{2n}$, the right block column gives $AF+BH=0$ and $CF+DH=I$. Therefore
$$\begin{bmatrix}A&B\\C&D\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}I&F\\0&H\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}A&AF+BH\\C&CF+DH\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}A&0\\C&I\end{bmatrix}.$$
Both $\begin{bmatrix}I&F\\0&H\end{bmatrix}$ and $\begin{bmatrix}A&0\\C&I\end{bmatrix}$ are block triangular, so their determinants are $\det I\cdot\det H=\det H$ and $\det A\cdot\det I=\det A$. Taking determinants of the identity above gives $\det M\cdot\det H=\det A$. ∎

imc-1997-08.title: Schur complement and continuity
imc-1997-08.body:
If $A$ is invertible, block elimination gives $M=\begin{bmatrix}I&0\\CA^{-1}&I\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}A&B\\0&D-CA^{-1}B\end{bmatrix}$, so $\det M=\det A\cdot\det S$ with $S=D-CA^{-1}B$, and the standard block-inverse formula gives $H=S^{-1}$. Hence $\det M\det H=\det A$.

If $A$ is singular, replace $A$ by $A+tI$ for small $t\ne0$: then $A+tI$ is invertible and (for $|t|$ small) $M_t$ is still invertible; the lower-right block $H_t$ of $M_t^{-1}$ depends continuously on $t$. The identity $\det M_t\det H_t=\det(A+tI)$ for all small $t\ne0$ passes to the limit $t\to0$. ∎

imc-1997-09.title: Pair the terms; the terms do not vanish for $\alpha\le0$
imc-1997-09.body:
Let $f(t)=\dfrac{\sin(\log t)}{t^\alpha}$ for $t\ge1$.

**$\alpha>0$: convergence.** We have
$$f'(t)=\frac{\cos(\log t)-\alpha\sin(\log t)}{t^{\alpha+1}},\qquad |f'(t)|\le\frac{1+\alpha}{t^{\alpha+1}}.$$
By the mean value theorem, $|f(2k-1)-f(2k)|\le\sup_{[2k-1,2k]}|f'|\le\frac{1+\alpha}{(2k-1)^{\alpha+1}}$, and $\sum_k(2k-1)^{-\alpha-1}<\infty$ because $\alpha+1>1$. So the partial sums
$$S_{2N}=\sum_{k=1}^N\bigl(f(2k-1)-f(2k)\bigr)$$
converge. Moreover $|f(n)|\le n^{-\alpha}\to0$, so $S_{2N+1}=S_{2N}+f(2N+1)$ has the same limit. Hence the series converges.

**$\alpha\le0$: divergence.** Then $|f(n)|\ge|\sin(\log n)|$ for $n\ge1$, so it suffices to show that $\sin(\log n)\not\to0$. For each integer $k\ge0$ consider
$$I_k=\bigl[e^{2\pi k+\pi/4},\ e^{2\pi k+3\pi/4}\bigr].$$
Its length is $e^{2\pi k+\pi/4}(e^{\pi/2}-1)>1$, so it contains an integer $n_k$, and $\log n_k\in[2\pi k+\frac\pi4,2\pi k+\frac{3\pi}4]$ gives $\sin(\log n_k)\ge\frac{\sqrt2}2$. Thus infinitely many terms have absolute value $\ge\frac{\sqrt2}2$; the terms do not tend to $0$ and the series diverges. ∎

imc-1997-10.title: Evaluate on matrix units
imc-1997-10.body:
Let $E_{ij}$ be the matrix with $1$ in position $(i,j)$ and $0$ elsewhere; they form a basis of $M_n$, and $E_{ij}E_{kl}=\delta_{jk}E_{il}$.

**a)** For any $C=(c_{ij})$, $\operatorname{tr}(AC)=\sum_{i}\sum_j a_{ij}c_{ji}$. Define $C$ by $c_{ji}=f(E_{ij})$. Then by linearity
$$f(A)=f\Bigl(\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}E_{ij}\Bigr)=\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}f(E_{ij})=\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}c_{ji}=\operatorname{tr}(AC).$$
Uniqueness: if $\operatorname{tr}(AC)=\operatorname{tr}(AC')$ for all $A$, then with $D=C-C'$ and $A=E_{ij}$ we get $0=\operatorname{tr}(E_{ij}D)=d_{ji}$ for all $i,j$, so $C=C'$.

**b)** For $i\ne j$: $E_{ij}=E_{ii}E_{ij}$ while $E_{ij}E_{ii}=0$, so by (2) $f(E_{ij})=f(E_{ii}E_{ij})=f(E_{ij}E_{ii})=f(0)=0$. For any $i,j$: $E_{ij}E_{ji}=E_{ii}$ and $E_{ji}E_{ij}=E_{jj}$, so $f(E_{ii})=f(E_{jj})$; call this common value $\lambda$. Then
$$f(A)=\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}f(E_{ij})=\lambda\sum_ia_{ii}=\lambda\operatorname{tr}(A).\ \blacksquare$$

imc-1997-10.title: Use the matrix $C$ from part a)
imc-1997-10.body: For b), write $f(X)=\operatorname{tr}(XC)$. Then (2) says $\operatorname{tr}(ABC)=\operatorname{tr}(BAC)=\operatorname{tr}(ACB)$ (cyclicity), i.e. $\operatorname{tr}\bigl(A(BC-CB)\bigr)=0$ for all $A$. By the uniqueness in a), $BC-CB=0$ for every $B$: $C$ commutes with all matrices. Taking $B=E_{ij}$: $E_{ij}C=CE_{ij}$; comparing entries, $(E_{ij}C)_{il}=c_{jl}$ and $(CE_{ij})_{il}=c_{ii}\delta_{jl}$, so $c_{jl}=0$ for $l\ne j$ and $c_{jj}=c_{ii}$. Thus $C=\lambda I$ and $f(A)=\operatorname{tr}(\lambda A)=\lambda\operatorname{tr}A$. ∎

imc-1997-11.title: Reflections on each orbit
imc-1997-11.body:
Write $f^k$ for the $k$-th iterate ($k\in\mathbb Z$; $f^0=\mathrm{id}$, $f^{-k}=(f^{-1})^k$), which makes sense because $f$ is a bijection. For $x\in X$ let $T(x)=\{f^k(x):k\in\mathbb Z\}$ be its orbit. Two orbits are equal or disjoint, so $X$ is a disjoint union of orbits, each mapped onto itself by $f$. It is enough to define $g_1,g_2$ on each orbit separately.

Choose (axiom of choice) a base point $x_0$ in each orbit $T$. Every element of $T$ is $f^k(x_0)$ for some $k\in\mathbb Z$. If $T$ is infinite, $k$ is unique; if $T$ is finite with $m$ elements, then $f^k(x_0)=f^l(x_0)$ iff $k\equiv l\pmod m$. Define on $T$
$$g_2\bigl(f^k(x_0)\bigr)=f^{-k}(x_0),\qquad g_1\bigl(f^k(x_0)\bigr)=f^{1-k}(x_0).$$
These are well defined: if $k\equiv l\pmod m$ then $-k\equiv-l$ and $1-k\equiv1-l\pmod m$. Now
- $g_2(g_2(f^k(x_0)))=f^{k}(x_0)$ and $g_1(g_1(f^k(x_0)))=f^{1-(1-k)}(x_0)=f^k(x_0)$, so $g_1\circ g_1=g_2\circ g_2=\mathrm{id}$;
- $g_1(g_2(f^k(x_0)))=g_1(f^{-k}(x_0))=f^{1+k}(x_0)=f\bigl(f^k(x_0)\bigr)$, so $g_1\circ g_2=f$.

(Geometrically: on a finite orbit $f$ is a rotation of a regular $m$-gon and on an infinite orbit it is the shift $k\mapsto k+1$ of $\mathbb Z$; both are compositions of two reflections, $k\mapsto-k$ followed by $k\mapsto1-k$.) ∎

imc-1997-12.title: Signed distance to the Cantor set
imc-1997-12.body:
**a)** Let $f(x)=x\sin\frac1x$ for $x\in(0,1]$ and $f(0)=0$; $f$ is continuous since $|f(x)|\le x$. Its zeros in $(0,1]$ are $x_k=\frac1{k\pi}$, $k\ge1$, and near each $x_k$ the factor $\sin\frac1x$ changes sign while $x>0$, so $f$ takes both signs in every neighbourhood of $x_k$. Thus $f$ crosses the axis at infinitely many points (also at $0$).

**b) Yes.** Let $C\subset[0,1]$ be the Cantor set: $C_0=[0,1]$, and $C_k$ is obtained from $C_{k-1}$ (a union of $2^{k-1}$ closed intervals of length $3^{-(k-1)}$) by removing the open middle third of each interval; $C=\bigcap_kC_k$. Call the $2^{k-1}$ removed open intervals the intervals *of stage $k$*; $[0,1]\setminus C$ is the disjoint union of all of them. $C$ is closed and uncountable: $C$ consists of the numbers $\sum_{j\ge1}b_j3^{-j}$ with $b_j\in\{0,2\}$, and $(b_j)\mapsto\sum b_j3^{-j}$ is injective on such digit sequences, so $C$ is in bijection with the set of all $0$–$1$ sequences.

Define
$$f(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\in C,\\(-1)^k\operatorname{dist}(x,C),&x\text{ in an interval of stage }k.\end{cases}$$
*Continuity.* $x\mapsto\operatorname{dist}(x,C)$ is continuous (1-Lipschitz). On each removed open interval $f=\pm\operatorname{dist}(\cdot,C)$ with a fixed sign, hence continuous there. At $c\in C$: $|f(x)-f(c)|=|f(x)|\le\operatorname{dist}(x,C)\le|x-c|$. So $f$ is continuous on $[0,1]$.

*Crossing.* Let $c\in C$ and $\delta>0$. Choose $K$ with $3^{-K}<\delta$. The point $c$ lies in one of the closed intervals $J$ of $C_K$, which has length $3^{-K}$, so $J\subset(c-\delta,c+\delta)$. The middle third of $J$ is an interval of stage $K+1$, and the middle third of the left third of $J$ is an interval of stage $K+2$; both lie in $J$. On them $\operatorname{dist}(\cdot,C)>0$ and $f$ has the signs $(-1)^{K+1}$ and $(-1)^{K+2}$, i.e. both signs occur in $(c-\delta,c+\delta)$. Since $f(c)=0$, $f$ crosses the axis at every point of $C$ — uncountably many points. ∎
